title: When air has two jobs inside a robot
lead: UC San Diego engineers used compressed air to open and close air passages and then move six soft legs. Their printed robot reached 4.72 meters per second in testing.

news.title: What a soft robot borrowed from a steam engine
news.summary: UC San Diego engineers printed a six-legged robot that runs on compressed air. To reach up to 4.72 meters per second, they made one flow of air do two jobs in turn.
news.details: The legs and pneumatic mechanism were printed in one soft material.
news.technical_novelty: Air switches the valves first and moves the legs next, following a principle used in compound steam engines.
news.engineering_impact: The team tried the machine on several surfaces and in water.
news.limitations: A hose still connects it to its air supply.
news.evidence_status: The researchers and the university describe physical tests.
news.body:
The six legs on a soft robot built at UC San Diego move on compressed air. The team wanted to speed up this kind of running machine and reached a reported top speed of 4.72 meters per second. The team printed the body in one piece, with passages that guide air through the robot like pipes carrying water through a building.

The body contains valves, chambers and tubes. The team enlarged and strengthened the design to handle higher pressure and flow. To make better use of the expanding air, the researchers borrowed the principle behind the compound steam engine. Compressed air first works in small, high-pressure chambers to run the valves. It then goes to larger, lower-pressure chambers and drives the legs.

The team’s earlier design moved at 4 centimeters per second. The new robot reached up to 4.72 meters per second. The university says the team tested it on concrete, gravel, grass, mulch and sand. It also went down stairs, swam and moved underwater. The robot works with a hose tether to an external source of compressed air.

The order of events is worth following. A valve opens or closes an air passage. After the air has done that first job, it still has energy to push against part of a leg. The researchers put that energy to work in the next chamber. The idea goes back to engines in which steam continued to expand from one cylinder into another. Here the sequence happens inside a printed body. Finding a way to carry the air supply remains an open design task: the six-legged runner used a tether during testing.

news.title: How a two-armed robot earns credit before the board is in place
news.summary: Canada’s Bagel Labs published a breakdown of how a program controls two robot arms. The virtual RoboDojo-Sim test awards credit for progress toward a goal, so a model’s ranking and its rate of finished tasks reveal different things.
news.details: Two simulated grippers lift a board together and lower it onto supports in a documented example.
news.technical_novelty: The model refreshes its plan from three camera views and the robot’s state.
news.engineering_impact: Category scores show where the model more often finishes a task.
news.limitations: The published scores come from simulation.
news.evidence_status: Bagel Labs published code and a breakdown of its results.
news.body:
A robot trying to lay a board across two supports can fail at different moments: one gripper might miss an edge, or the board might come down past a support. Canada’s Bagel Labs showed this task in RoboDojo-Sim, a computer environment where programs operate virtual robots. The team released code for its Bagel-Robotics-1 model along with a breakdown of its performance. In one recorded run the robot picked up the board with both hands and laid it across the supports.

The model receives a task instruction, views from one head camera and two wrist cameras, and the robot's current state. It predicts 32 actions in a batch, executes 16 and then makes a new plan from fresh observations. That refresh lets the next prediction account for where the arms and objects are after the previous burst of movement.

In Bagel Labs' November 20 snapshot of RoboDojo-Sim, the model placed third among models evaluated without a separate software agent. It averaged 38.65 points out of 100, with an average full-task success rate of 31.91%. It completed 3.33% of trials in the Open category, which includes open-ended tasks and tasks guided by text or images. The ranking awards partial credit and gives each of the five main categories the same weight.

A partial score helps a researcher see whether a new control program is getting any closer to its goal after a string of failures. The full completion rate answers a separate question: how often did it get all the way there? For the board example, Bagel Labs publishes settings for one successful run. The recording lets you trace how the two arms move together. To see how often the policy finishes work, look at the completion rates across the test rather than the recording of that single run.

news.title: How a delivery robot gets past a locked apartment entrance
news.summary: Four companies tested apartment deliveries in a residential building in Fukuoka. They connected a robot to the intercom, building access system and elevator and tested leaving a parcel outside when the resident was away.
news.details: The November 18 test took place in Building 3 of a residential complex in Kashii, Fukuoka.
news.technical_novelty: The robot works with the intercom, delivery access system and elevator.
news.engineering_impact: When nobody is home, a drop-off lets the resident collect the parcel later.
news.limitations: The participants did not publish a route completion rate.
news.evidence_status: World Supply and NETSDAR Robot Solutions described the trial.
news.organization: Aiphone, NETSDAR Robot Solutions, Nippon Otis Elevator and World Supply
news.body:
Could a robot take a parcel through a locked entrance, get to the right floor and finish the delivery even if nobody is home? NETSDAR Robot Solutions, Aiphone, Nippon Otis Elevator and World Supply tested that kind of apartment delivery in Fukuoka on November 18. The partners examined whether a robot could carry a parcel to a resident’s door and leave it there when needed.

Wheels solve only part of the problem. In a building with controlled entry, the delivery needs to work with the intercom and the system that unlocks the entrance. For travel between floors the robot also has to work with the elevator. The housing agency’s test plan shows the courier using delivery paperwork with the intercom to unlock the entrance, then handing the parcel over in the lobby. Once it has the parcel, the robot takes the elevator to the right floor.

A trial in the previous year had already looked at front-door delivery. This year the robot supplier said the partners added intercom integration, a drop-off option and a logistics company to the test. Leaving a parcel has a specific purpose: saving the courier another trip. The participants did not disclose how many deliveries finished without a return visit.

news.title: Where a parcel’s flight begins and ends
news.summary: Local authorities and companies in Shinshiro, Japan, tested three routes for flying medicines to recipients. One drone started out empty and landed near a pharmacy to collect a box before it flew on.
news.details: In one trial flight the drone carried a box to a nursing home in about 12 minutes.
news.technical_novelty: Another route included a landing at a pharmacy for loading.
news.engineering_impact: The routes test which jobs fall to pharmacy staff and which to the recipient.
news.limitations: Flight times were reported separately from work on the ground.
news.evidence_status: Project partners and the industry publication LNEWS described the trial.
news.organization: Aichi Prefecture, Shinshiro, Aeronext and Green Service
news.body:
Does a medicine-carrying drone get its box before it takes off, or collect it at a pharmacy on the way? Aichi Prefecture and Shinshiro tried both arrangements with Aeronext and Green Service. They wanted to see how to connect a flight to preparing a package and handing it over to staff at a nursing home. The organizers released details of three routes on November 20.

In the public demonstration on November 18, a pharmacy brought the medicine by road to the launch site at Yokogawa community center. The crew loaded a box onto the drone. According to the organizers, it flew about eight kilometers in roughly 12 minutes to a nursing home, where staff collected the package. The time given was for the flight from the launch site to the destination.

On a different route, the aircraft left the hub empty, landed near a pharmacy for staff to load a box and flew on to a second nursing home. The organizers put the two outbound legs at about 13 and five minutes respectively, excluding the return. Local medical logistics company Green Service ran the flights, with remote operations based in Tsushima.

At the pharmacy stop, pharmacy staff could fasten a sealed box to the aircraft themselves. Staff at the destination had their own part to play. The partners developed a special box that a registered nurse could unlock with a fingerprint, so the intended recipient could open it after the box had been dropped off. The report gives the time in the air on individual legs. It leaves open how long it took staff to reach the aircraft and complete the handoff on the ground.

news.title: What records can reveal about a shipment of NVIDIA chips
news.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS that the administration had contacted the interim leadership of chipmaker NVIDIA. He explained why shipping and payment records could help officials examine sales to China.
news.details: Officials want to establish who handled export compliance inside NVIDIA.
news.technical_novelty: Shipping and payment records can help connect a consignment with a transaction.
news.engineering_impact: Computing chips from suppliers such as NVIDIA also help robotics developers train control models.
news.limitations: Officials are still examining what happened and who was involved.
news.evidence_status: The CBS transcript and a Reuters report document the administration’s contacts.
news.organization: US Department of the Treasury and NVIDIA
news.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS on November 22 that the administration had been in touch with NVIDIA’s interim leadership. The company makes chips for demanding computing jobs, including training programs to control robots by learning from many examples. Officials are asking about shipments of chips to China and who inside the company was responsible for following export rules.

Bessent said the administration had contacted NVIDIA’s interim leadership, board directors and lawyers. At the time of the interview, he said it was still waiting for the answers it wanted. He said officials wanted to find out who was responsible for compliance with export rules and what levels of the company knew about shipments under scrutiny.

Bessent pointed to shipping and payment records as a way to reconstruct transactions even where arrangements were informal. He described possible systemic noncompliance as something still being looked into. Reuters also reported the contacts. NVIDIA’s board announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned and that chief financial officer Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO. Bessent confirmed that the chief financial officer was in charge.

A shipment of expensive equipment creates records in different places. Shipping documents can identify who sent the goods and what was shipped, while payment records track the money. Putting those records together helps officials piece together part of the story and find out who could authorize a transaction. Bessent identified one specific question: what employees knew about the shipments under review, and whether that knowledge reached the people running the company.

technology_signal.title: Two stages of work for compressed air
technology_signal.summary: In UC San Diego’s six-legged robot, the same air first opens and closes passages and then pushes the legs. The researchers borrowed the idea from compound steam engines.
technology_signal.implications: The prototype uses air supplied through a hose. The team is exploring whether a future version could use a small portable air cartridge.
